title: The Last Ember Again
premise: Paloma Ashgrove, a mercenary bound to the silent god Vesper and keeper of the Gilded Ledger guild's impossible inventory, finds his own name and tonight's date inscribed in a prophecy book a century old. The prophecy foretells that a soul sold to the Ember Court beneath the mountain will be consumed at the turning of the season—and that soul belongs to Wren, the pickpocket girl the guild raised as their own. Paloma assembles a crew of ledger-debtors and disgraced oathkeepers to steal Wren's soul back from a court that trades in names, memories, and fire. In the end, Paloma learns the silent god never abandoned him: it poured itself into the ledger, and into him, and he must choose between restoring his god and spending that divine ember to buy Wren's freedom. He spends it, becoming the last ember himself—mortal, unmarked, and finally belonging to a family instead of a faith.
about_author: Zephyrine Montrose is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing guild records in mountain towns before turning to fiction. She writes fantasies about paperwork, oaths, and the people who fall through the cracks of both.

chapters.title: The Ledger Opens Both Ways
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He audits the guild's strangest inventory—a bottled thunderstorm, a debt of one honest tear—while dodging questions about his silent god. When a client pays in prophecy, he finds tonight's date and his own name inked a century ago. The emotional beat is the chill of a careful man realizing his invisibility was always someone else's design.

chapters.title: Wren Sings in the Dark
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The guild's adopted pickpocket hums a song she's never been taught, and old members go pale hearing it. Paloma realizes the melody is the anthem of the Ember Court. The beat is warm found-family banter curdling into dread as Paloma understands the prophecy's stolen soul wears his little sister's face.

chapters.title: Debtors of the Gilded Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He calls in favors from three people who owe the guild: Marisol the oathbreaker knight, Tetch the cartographer of places that move, and Brother Quill, a priest who worships Vesper wrong. The beat is reluctant camaraderie—each debtor joining not for debt but because they, too, were abandoned by something they loved.

chapters.title: What the Mountain Remembers
chapters.summary: Tetch's POV. The crew travels the shifting pass beneath Mount Cendre, navigating roads that rearrange to keep secrets. Tetch confesses she once mapped the Ember Court and had the memory sold out of her. The beat is vertigo and trust: the crew must literally hold hands through unmappable ground.

chapters.title: The Toll of Names
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the mountain's gate, a ferryman demands a name as toll. Marisol surrenders her knighthood's name; Paloma offers a false one and it burns him, proof the Court can taste lies. The beat is sacrifice as currency, and the first hint that Paloma's true name is worth more than he knows.

chapters.title: Court Beneath the Mountain
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Ember Court is a cathedral of banked fires where courtiers trade memories like coins and the Queen of Cinders wears a crown of spent vows. Paloma poses as an appraiser. The beat is seductive horror—he is tempted by a memory of Vesper speaking to him, priced at a friend's name.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Was Sold
chapters.summary: Brother Quill's POV. Quill uncovers the guild's oldest ledger page: Wren's soul was pawned by her birth parents a century ago, held in trust until the season turns. The beat is grief and rage—Quill, who worships a silent god, must decide whether to tell Wren the truth or shield her with a lie.

chapters.title: Wren Refuses to Be Rescued
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren has followed them, disguised as a court scullery maid, and confronts Paloma: it's her soul, her choice. She reveals the Court offered her anything if she stays. The beat is defiant agency—the found family learns rescue without consent is just another kind of selling.

chapters.title: Auction of Impossible Things
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Court holds its centennial auction; the lot is 'one soul, lightly worn, maturing at season's turn.' Paloma bids the bottled thunderstorm and loses to a courtier bidding a century of borrowed time. The beat is public humiliation masking a private plan—he came to map the vault, not win.

chapters.title: Marisol Breaks Her Oath Properly
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The Court offers to restore Marisol's lost knighthood if she betrays the crew. She accepts, then uses her reinstated authority to unlock the vault doors before her betrayal is discovered. The beat is a woman choosing which vow matters, and the cost of being clever with your own damnation.

chapters.title: The Vault of Spent Fire
chapters.summary: Tetch's POV. Inside the vault, souls hang like lanterns. Tetch finds her sold memory in a jar and, reading it, remembers the Court's one weakness: the Queen cannot touch a soul freely given back. The beat is vertigo of recovered selfhood—she remembers who she was and chooses to keep going anyway.

chapters.title: The Queen of Cinders Offers a Bargain
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Cornered, Paloma is brought before the Queen, who reveals the prophecy's author: Vesper himself, who sold his voice to the Court a century ago and has been silent ever since. The Queen offers Wren's soul for Vesper's ember, which she believes sleeps in Paloma. The beat is the floor dropping out of his faith.

chapters.title: My God Was a Ledger All Along
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback-laced. He realizes every 'impossible thing' he's catalogued carries a spark of Vesper—the god didn't go silent; he scattered himself into the guild's inventory to hide from the Court. The beat is devastating tenderness: Paloma has been keeping his god's ashes on a shelf for years.

chapters.title: Quill's Heresy
chapters.summary: Brother Quill's POV. Quill argues they should restore Vesper—worship demands it. Paloma refuses to spend the ember on a god when it could save Wren. The crew splits. The beat is theology as family argument, and Quill quietly deciding his faith means siding with Paloma against his own church.

chapters.title: The Season Turns Tonight
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The Court begins the consumption rite early; Wren feels her edges fraying. She escapes her gilded cell using the pickpocket skills her family gave her, stealing the one thing no one guards: the Queen's own first memory. The beat is the apprentice out-thieving the masters.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Bridge of Ash
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The Court catches Marisol's double-dealing; to save the crew's escape she duels her old commander on a bridge of cooling cinders. The beat is bittersweet triumph—she wins, loses the restored name anyway, and finds she no longer wants it.

chapters.title: The Queen's First Memory
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Wren trades the Queen's memory for her soul's release, but the memory reveals the Queen was the first person Vesper ever loved, and she sold his voice out of jealousy. The Court's whole economy was built on one broken heart. The beat is pity for the monster.

chapters.title: Everything Burns Down to Choice
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The Court, destabilized by the Queen's grief, begins to collapse. Paloma holds Vesper's ember—enough to restore his god or free Wren—and the prophecy's final line appears in his hand: 'the last ember chooses.' The beat is stillness at the center of the fire.

chapters.title: The Last Ember
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. He pours Vesper's ember into Wren, spending his god a second time—once silent, now gone. Vesper's final voice, brief and warm, thanks him. The Court crumbles as the Queen, weeping, lets them go. The beat is sacrifice transfigured into inheritance: Paloma becomes what Vesper was.

chapters.title: What We Carried Out
chapters.summary: Tetch's POV. The crew emerges into dawn, changed: Marisol nameless and lighter, Quill heretic and content, Tetch whole, Wren carrying a god's spark. They take one jar from the ruins—the bottled thunderstorm—because some impossible things should survive. The beat is exhaustion laced with wonder.

chapters.title: A New Page in the Gilded Ledger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Back at the guild, Wren opens a fresh ledger and writes the crew's names as assets: 'not for sale, not at any price.' Paloma, no longer sworn to anything, asks what he is now. The beat is quiet joy—the answer is simply 'family,' written in ink that doesn't burn.

chapters.title: The Ember Keeps Its Own Books
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, coda. Months later, Paloma hears Vesper's warmth flicker in small mercies—a candle that won't die, a hearth that welcomes strangers. The god isn't restored; he's distributed. Paloma writes the first entry of a new prophecy book and leaves tonight's date blank. The beat is hope as an open ledger: the future unwritten, held by found hands.
